title: Intentional or inadvertent fake news sharing? Fact-checking warnings and users' interaction with social media content
screen_reason: Mixed-methods study (5 focus groups + an online survey in the Canary Islands, Spain, 28 March - 3 April 2020). The focus-group half is qualitative and yields nothing, but Study 2 reports, in Table 2 and in the text, the SHARE OF RESPONDENTS who say they shared COVID-19 news that was made up/false or exaggerated, both unaware (unintentional) and aware (intentional) - self-reported, observed behaviour in the weeks before the survey, not a hypothetical intention. That is RECALL with recall_subtype=sharing under the instructions ('share of survey respondents who say they ... SHARED misinformation'). Denominators are given as a percentage split of the sample with item non-response stated.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Study 1 (five focus groups, 31 participants, 10-12 March 2020) is wholly qualitative - transcript quotations only, no shares - so it produces no rows. (2) Table 1 reports mean TRUST in nine news sources on a 4-point scale (social media M = 1.79, instant messaging M = 1.66, newspapers M = 2.77 ...). These are scale means, not shares of respondents, and trust is not exposure to misinformation - no row per the instructions' 'scale MEANS only' exclusion. (3) Table 4 compares intentional distributors with the rest on gender (44.40% women among distributors vs 52.20%), age, education, ideology strength, trust in government and COVID-19 concern: these are demographic composition figures, not misinformation prevalence, so no rows; the only thing taken from Table 4 is its note, which supplies the missing denominator (108 + 343 = 451). (4) The UK figures the paper quotes from Chadwick, Vaccari & O'Loughlin (2018) - 17.1% 'exaggerated' and 8.9% 'made up' - are excluded under R8 as values cited from elsewhere. (5) Denominator ambiguity flagged in the notes of the 23.9% row: Abstract 'N = 350' vs Methods '471 valid responses' vs Table 4's implied 451. (6) The two composites (51.2%, 23.9%) and their component items are alternative levels of the SAME measurement; they overlap and must not both be pooled.

rob.design: Two studies. Study 1: 5 focus groups, 31 participants recruited from a Tenerife opinion-company panel, grouped by age and left/centre/right ideology, 10-12 March 2020, paid EUR 30, moderated/recorded/transcribed by the survey firm; stimuli were three real Facebook posts covered by a grey overlay and labelled 'false'/'partly false ... checked by independent fact-checkers'; qualitative only, no coding reliability reported. Study 2: online survey, LimeSurvey, 28 March - 3 April 2020, of Canary Islands residents 16+, administered by the same firm to its consumer panel and shared on the firm's social media (self-described convenience sample, younger and more educated than the population register); 471 valid responses to the news-use/fake-news block; item non-response 4.2% on each sharing item; blocks 2 and 3 were of voluntary response. No response rate is reported and no probability sampling frame exists. Measurement: 5 self-report frequency items (1 = never to 6), factor-analysed into intentional (3 items, alpha = .87) and unintentional (2 items) dimensions, 84.56% of variance, KMO = .741, factors correlated r = .50. Main risks: self-report and recall bias, social-desirability bias on the intentional items (acknowledged by the authors), non-probability sample, and an unreconciled sample size (350 vs 471 vs 451).
rob.item6_quote: Throughout the coronavirus crisis, how often have you shared news about the disease that… (a) seemed accurate at the time, but you later found was made up or false? (a) was exaggerated, and you were not aware of this? (b) you suspected was made up when you shared it? (b) was exaggerated, and you were aware of this? (b) you knew was made up or false at the time?
rob.item10_quote: However, taking 'a' items together, it is noteworthy that 51.2% of the respondents reported having shared "made up or false" or "exaggerated" content during the weeks before the survey without being aware of it at the time. More strikingly, 23.9% of respondents shared "made up or false" or "exaggerated" content online (group of 'b' items) at some point, and they were more or less aware of the problem.
